title: Readiness Status Report
instruction: Brief your superior officer on your unit's current operational readiness. Report on personnel numbers, equipment status, and any factors affecting your ability to carry out your assigned tasks.
preparationPoints: Current number of personnel available for duty
Any ongoing maintenance or training affecting readiness
Your unit's capacity to respond if tasked now
Any support or resources you need from higher

title: Base Orientation Briefing
instruction: A new officer is joining your unit next week. Give a briefing covering the base layout, daily routine, key facilities, and any procedures they need to know from day one.
preparationPoints: Location of key buildings (HQ, mess, accommodation, medical)
Points of contact for common issues
Any rules or local procedures that may be unfamiliar

title: Supply Resupply Request Brief
instruction: You are preparing for a three-day field exercise next week and your unit has identified several items that need to be resupplied before departure. Brief your platoon commander on what supplies are needed, why they are required, and what action you are requesting.
preparationPoints: Types of supplies needed (rations, batteries, fuel, medical kit)
Why resupply is necessary before the exercise
Your specific request to the commander

title: After-Action Exercise Brief
instruction: Your unit has just completed a two-day field training exercise. Give a brief summary to your section on how it went. Cover what the exercise objectives were, describe two things that went well, describe one thing that did not go as planned, and finish by stating one lesson your section should remember before the next exercise.
preparationPoints: Two specific things that went well
One thing that did not go as planned
One concrete lesson for the next exercise
What the section should do differently

title: Unit Movement Order Brief
instruction: Your unit is relocating to a new training area next week. Brief your soldiers on the key details of the movement: departure time and location, the route, what personal kit they must carry, vehicle allocation, and what behaviour is expected during transit.

title: Base Security Briefing for Visitors
instruction: A group of civilian officials from a partner government ministry will be visiting your base for a half-day tour. Before the tour begins, brief them on the base security rules: what areas are off-limits, photography restrictions, emergency procedures, and how they should behave throughout the visit. Your briefing must be clear and professional for a non-military audience.
preparationPoints: Areas of the base that are off-limits to visitors
Who to contact if they have questions or problems

title: Training Incident Briefing
instruction: You are the duty officer. Brief your commander on a training incident that occurred this morning. Cover what happened, who was involved, immediate consequences, and the actions already taken.
preparationPoints: What you recommend as next steps

title: Pre-Deployment Intelligence Briefing
instruction: Before your unit deploys on a peacekeeping mission, brief your section on the intelligence picture. Cover the security environment, key actors, potential threats, and how this shapes your rules of engagement.
preparationPoints: General security situation in the area of operations
Key armed groups or actors and their intentions
Most likely and most dangerous threat scenarios
How the intelligence picture affects your mission
Information gaps and what to watch for on the ground

title: Operational Readiness Briefing
instruction: You are presenting at a command-level meeting. Brief senior commanders on your formation's readiness to execute its assigned operation, including capability gaps, risk assessment, and your recommended timeline.
preparationPoints: Current state of readiness across key capability areas
Identified gaps and their operational impact
Risk level if the operation proceeds as planned
Mitigation measures already in place or requested
Recommended timeline and any conditions that must be met

title: Section Development Brief
instruction: Brief your commanding officer on the professional development status of your section or platoon. Cover individual performance against their current role, which personnel you consider ready for promotion or additional responsibility, which individuals need targeted development and why, and your plan to develop the section's overall capability over the next quarter.
preparationPoints: Overall performance assessment of the section
Personnel ready for promotion or additional responsibility
Personnel requiring targeted development and the reason
Your development plan for the next quarter
Resources or support needed from higher command

title: Operation Order Brief
instruction: You are about to conduct a complex security operation in an area with a mixed civilian and military presence. Brief your platoon or section using a structured operation order format. Cover the situation (ground, enemy, and friendly forces), your mission statement, your concept of operations, the tasks of each element, and the key coordination instructions they need before the operation begins.
preparationPoints: Situation — ground, enemy forces, friendly forces
Mission statement — who, what, when, where, why
Concept of operations — how the mission will be achieved
Coordination instructions — timings, communications, actions on

title: End-of-Tour Strategic Assessment
instruction: You are briefing your higher commander at the end of a six-month operational deployment. Provide a strategic assessment of what was achieved against the original mandate, where the mission fell short of its objectives and why, the key lessons your deployment identified that should inform the planning of future operations in this environment, and your specific recommendations for both the incoming unit and the higher command's strategy going forward.
preparationPoints: Assessment of what was achieved against the mandate
Where the mission fell short and the reasons
Specific recommendations for the incoming unit
Recommendations to higher command for strategic planning

title: Patrol Status Report
instruction: You are on patrol and need to report your status back to base. Give a SITREP covering your current position, what you have observed, any contacts made, and your intended next movement.
preparationPoints: Your current grid reference or position description
Any contacts or incidents to report
Your planned next action or route

title: Border Observation Report
instruction: You are manning an observation post on the border. Report to your operations centre on what you have observed during the past two hours, including any movement, vehicles, or persons of interest.
preparationPoints: Time and location of your observation
Volume and type of activity observed

title: Vehicle Breakdown SITREP
instruction: Your vehicle has broken down on the route to a supply point, five kilometres from base. Give a SITREP to your operations room covering your position, the nature of the breakdown, the status of your personnel, the impact on your mission, and what assistance you are requesting.
preparationPoints: What support or assistance you need

title: Casualty Report SITREP
instruction: During a foot patrol, one of your soldiers has badly injured their ankle on uneven ground and cannot walk without support. Report the incident to your company command post covering: your location, the nature and severity of the injury, how it occurred, what first aid has been given, the soldier's current condition, and what you need from command.
preparationPoints: Nature and severity of the injury

title: Weather Delay SITREP
instruction: Severe rain and reduced visibility have significantly slowed your convoy during a resupply mission. Give a SITREP to your commanding officer covering your current position, the weather conditions affecting movement, your revised estimated time of arrival, any safety concerns, and whether you are requesting permission to halt or to continue at reduced speed.
preparationPoints: Current position and progress so far
Weather conditions and how they affect movement
Safety concerns for personnel or vehicles
Your request — halt and wait, or continue at reduced speed

title: Document Irregularity Checkpoint SITREP
instruction: Your checkpoint has stopped a civilian vehicle whose occupants are carrying identity documents that appear to be false. You have detained the vehicle and its two occupants for further investigation. Report the incident to your platoon commander covering: location and time, what raised your suspicion, what action you have taken, the current status of the detainees, and what guidance you need to proceed correctly.
preparationPoints: Location and time of the stop
Current status of the vehicle and detainees
Guidance needed from command to proceed

title: Civilian Contact Incident SITREP
instruction: Your patrol has had an unplanned contact with local civilians that resulted in a minor incident. Give a SITREP to your command element covering what happened, the immediate response, and the current situation.
preparationPoints: Time, location and nature of the contact
How the situation developed and actions taken
Casualties or damage — military and civilian
Current status and force protection posture

title: Civil Unrest SITREP
instruction: Civil unrest has broken out near your forward operating base. Provide a SITREP to your commander assessing the scale of the unrest, the threat it poses to your force, and your recommended immediate actions.
preparationPoints: Nature and scale of the unrest — numbers, weapons, direction of movement
Proximity to your base and current threat level
Actions already taken to secure the perimeter
Coordination with civilian authorities or police
Your recommended course of action and request to higher

title: Credible Threat SITREP
instruction: Your intelligence section has received information of a credible threat against your installation within the next 24 hours. Give a SITREP to your operations officer covering: the nature and assessed credibility of the threat and its source, your current force protection posture and any gaps in that posture, the measures you have already put in place, and what additional authority or resources you are requesting from command.
preparationPoints: Nature of the threat and its assessed credibility
Current force protection posture and identified gaps

title: IED Discovery SITREP
instruction: Your patrol has discovered a suspected IED on a main supply route. Report the discovery to your operations room covering: precise location and the indicators that caused you to suspect an IED, the immediate actions your patrol has taken to secure and isolate the area, the impact on vehicle movement along the route, and the specialist support you are requesting and within what timeframe you need it.
preparationPoints: Precise location of the suspected device
Immediate actions to secure and isolate the area
Impact on route and vehicle movement

title: Fratricide Incident SITREP
instruction: A fratricide incident has occurred in your sector — one of your unit's weapon systems has engaged what appears to have been a friendly force. You are the senior officer first on scene. Give an initial SITREP to your commander covering: what is confirmed and what is still uncertain, the immediate actions already taken, the casualty situation, your current force protection status, and your recommendation for the immediate reporting chain — including who outside the chain of command must be notified.
preparationPoints: What is confirmed — what weapon system, approximate time, location
What remains uncertain — cause, friendly force identification
Recommended reporting chain including legal and command notifications

title: Communications Equipment Failure
instruction: Your unit's primary communications equipment has failed during an exercise. Describe the problem to your superior, explain the operational impact, and propose immediate workarounds until the equipment is repaired.
preparationPoints: What has failed and possible reason for the failure
Which communications links are now unavailable
How this affects current and planned operations
Immediate workarounds or backup systems available
Who needs to be informed and what support you need

title: Accommodation Shortage
instruction: Your unit has just arrived at a forward location and there is not enough accommodation for all your personnel. Some soldiers will have to sleep in vehicles or improvised shelters overnight. Explain the problem to your superior and propose at least two options for managing the situation tonight.
preparationPoints: The welfare and rest impact on soldiers
Option 1 — priority allocation of available spaces
Option 2 — temporary use of vehicles or shelters
What you need from your superior

title: Interpreter Unavailable
instruction: Your assigned interpreter has fallen ill and will not be available for an important meeting with local community leaders scheduled for tomorrow morning. Explain the problem to your commanding officer, describe the operational impact, and propose at least two alternative solutions for how to proceed.
preparationPoints: Operational impact of the cancelled support
Any other practical alternative (bilingual soldier, written communication)

title: Convoy Vehicle Breakdown
instruction: One of your unit's vehicles has broken down during a road march, causing the convoy to fall behind schedule. You have cargo that must reach its destination by a fixed time. Report the situation to your superior and recommend how to proceed, giving at least two options and your preferred course of action.
preparationPoints: Which vehicle broke down and at what stage of the route
The impact on the convoy schedule
The cargo or task at risk
Option 1 — call for recovery and redistribute cargo
Option 2 — continue with remaining vehicles and return for the broken one

title: Medical Supply Shortage
instruction: Your forward post is running critically low on medical supplies, including bandages, pain relief medication, and IV fluid. Your next scheduled resupply is five days away but your current stock will last only two more days. Report the problem to your company commander, explain the risk to your personnel if supplies do not arrive in time, and propose at least two options to solve the problem before your supplies run out.
preparationPoints: Current stock levels and how long they will last
Risk to personnel if supplies are not received
Option 1 — emergency resupply by air or priority vehicle
Option 2 — local procurement or transfer from another unit

title: Natural Disaster Response
instruction: A natural disaster has occurred in your operational area. Describe how your unit would respond in the first 48 hours, coordinating with civilian authorities and international organisations.
preparationPoints: Resources available and how to deploy them
Coordination with civilian and international bodies
Chain of command and decision authority

title: Critical Supply Shortage
instruction: Your unit faces a critical supply shortage that will affect operations within 72 hours. Present the problem to your superior, propose alternative solutions, and recommend a course of action.
preparationPoints: Nature and scale of the shortage

title: Multinational Force Friction
instruction: During a joint operation, a serious misunderstanding between your troops and allied forces has created friction that is affecting mission performance. Describe the problem and propose a solution that preserves both the mission and the relationship.
preparationPoints: Nature of the misunderstanding and how it arose
Impact on the mission and the professional relationship
Cultural or procedural differences that contributed

title: Exercise Communications Breakdown
instruction: During a multinational exercise, a breakdown in the communications architecture has left several national contingents unable to receive orders. As the exercise controller, describe the problem and lead the recovery plan.
preparationPoints: Which contingents are affected and what they are missing
Root cause of the breakdown if known
Immediate workaround to restore command and control
Lessons identified for future exercise planning

title: Assuming Command in a Crisis
instruction: Your commanding officer has been medically evacuated during an active operation and communications with higher headquarters have failed. As the next in seniority, you must assume command immediately. Explain to your assembled section and team leaders how you are assuming command, confirm what the mission is and that it continues, clarify what decisions each team leader is authorised to take independently during the communications blackout, and state what your immediate priorities are.
preparationPoints: Confirmation that the mission continues unchanged
Decisions that team leaders are authorised to take independently
Your immediate priorities as new commander
Plan to re-establish communications with higher headquarters

title: Civilian Casualties After an Air Strike
instruction: An air strike in your operational area has resulted in civilian casualties. You are the ground force commander. Report the situation to your superior officer: describe what happened and the civilian casualty situation, assess the immediate reaction of the local population and the media environment, explain the actions already taken to address humanitarian and medical needs, and propose how you would manage the operational and reputational dimensions of the situation over the next 48 hours.
preparationPoints: What happened and the civilian casualty situation
Local population reaction and current media environment
Humanitarian and medical actions already taken
Operational management for the next 48 hours

title: Coalition Rules of Engagement Conflict
instruction: During a joint operation, you have discovered that your coalition partner's rules of engagement permit the use of force in circumstances where your own ROE would prohibit it. This discrepancy has already caused a near-incident. Explain the problem to your legal advisor and operations officer, describe the specific legal risk this creates for your national force, and propose at least two solutions that would allow the mission to continue while maintaining your country's legal obligations.
preparationPoints: The specific ROE discrepancy and the near-incident
Legal risk created for your national force
Solution 1 — separate operating areas or task deconfliction
Solution 2 — seek ROE harmonisation through the chain of command
How to maintain the mission while protecting national legal obligations

title: Disinformation Campaign Response
instruction: A coordinated disinformation campaign on social media is falsely attributing actions to your force that did not occur. The narrative is spreading rapidly and beginning to threaten the political legitimacy of your mission in the host nation. Brief your public affairs officer and commander on the nature and likely origin of the campaign, the operational and strategic consequences if it goes unchallenged, and a proposed response strategy across military, diplomatic, and media lines of effort.
preparationPoints: Nature of the disinformation and its likely origin
How the narrative is spreading and its current reach
Operational and strategic consequences if unchallenged
Military response — factual record and official rebuttal
Diplomatic and media response strategy across lines of effort

title: Leadership Under Pressure
instruction: Describe a situation in which a military leader must make a critical decision with incomplete information and limited time. Explain the decision-making process and the leadership principles involved.
preparationPoints: Communicating the decision to the team

title: Drones in Military Operations
instruction: Present the advantages and limitations of using unmanned aerial systems (drones) in modern military operations. Consider operational, ethical and legal dimensions.
preparationPoints: Ethical concerns and rules of engagement

title: Mandatory Language Training
instruction: Argue for or against making advanced English language training mandatory for all officers above the rank of captain. Support your argument with specific operational and institutional reasons.
preparationPoints: Operational necessity — when is English critical?
The link between language ability and career progression
Risks of insufficient language capability at senior level
Counterarguments and how to address them

title: AI in Military Decision-Making
instruction: To what extent should artificial intelligence be used in military decision-making? Present your position on the role of AI in planning, targeting, and command and control, and identify the key risks.
preparationPoints: Potential benefits of AI in planning and analysis
Specific domains where AI is already being used
Ethical and legal constraints on autonomous systems
The risk of over-reliance and algorithmic bias
Your view on the appropriate boundary for human judgement

title: Women in Combat Roles
instruction: Argue for the expanded integration of women into direct combat roles in your country's armed forces. Address the most common objections and explain how this would strengthen overall military capability.
preparationPoints: The experience of nations that have already expanded integration
How diversity of personnel strengthens mission capability
Addressing physical standards — what evidence shows
Cultural change and unit cohesion considerations
Legal and institutional obligations under international frameworks

title: Offensive Cyber Capabilities
instruction: Present your position on whether armed forces should develop and maintain offensive cyber capabilities as a standard element of their military doctrine. Address the operational utility of such capabilities, the legal constraints imposed by international humanitarian law, the risk of uncontrolled escalation, and whether such a capability strengthens or complicates a state's deterrence posture.
preparationPoints: Your clear position — for or against, with conditions
Operational utility — what offensive cyber can achieve
Legal constraints under IHL — distinction, proportionality, attribution
Escalation risks and how to manage them
Impact on deterrence posture — strengthening or complicating

title: Defence Budget Prioritisation
instruction: Your country's defence budget has been reduced by fifteen percent. Present your recommendation on which capability area should receive protected funding and which area can accept a reduction, justifying your priorities in terms of the most likely threat environment your country faces over the next decade. Address also the implications of your recommendation for your country's commitments within NATO or your regional alliance.
preparationPoints: Your recommendation — which capability to protect and which to reduce
Threat environment analysis for the next decade
Justification for protected capability — why it is essential
Justification for the reduction — why it is acceptable
Alliance commitment implications of your recommendation

title: Hybrid Warfare and Conventional Response
instruction: Argue that conventional military doctrine is insufficient on its own to deter or respond to hybrid warfare as practised by contemporary state actors. Identify the specific capability gaps that hybrid operations exploit, propose the measures — military and non-military — that should complement conventional force, and address the principal political and institutional obstacles to implementing those measures within a NATO or alliance framework.
preparationPoints: Why conventional doctrine has specific gaps against hybrid threats
The hybrid capabilities that exploit those gaps
Military measures to complement conventional force
Non-military measures — cyber, information, civil resilience
Political and institutional obstacles within NATO to implementing these measures

title: Military Vehicle Description
instruction: Describe a military vehicle you are familiar with. Cover its type, main characteristics, what it is used for, and any limitations an operator needs to be aware of.
preparationPoints: Name and type of the vehicle
Primary role and when it is used
One important limitation or maintenance consideration

title: Military Installation Layout
instruction: Describe the layout of a military base or installation you know. Explain where the key areas are located and how they relate to each other, as if you were orienting a new arrival.
preparationPoints: Location of headquarters and command element

title: Patrol Route Description
instruction: Describe a patrol route using map references, terrain features and key checkpoints. Your patrol commander will use your description to plan the route without having seen the map himself.
preparationPoints: Start point and direction of travel
Key terrain features along the route
Named checkpoints and what to observe at each

title: Equipment Briefing
instruction: Describe a piece of communications or medical equipment used in your unit. Explain what it does, how it is operated at a basic level, and what training is required to use it correctly.
preparationPoints: Name and purpose of the equipment
Common faults and how to identify them
Training or qualification required to operate it

title: Day Patrol Equipment
instruction: Describe the personal equipment that a soldier in your unit is required to carry on a standard day patrol. Name each item, explain what it is used for, and mention any important rules about how it must be maintained or carried.

title: Checkpoint Layout
instruction: Describe a vehicle checkpoint that your unit has set up on a main road. Explain the physical layout — where vehicles are stopped, where documents are checked, where searches are conducted — and explain how each part of the layout contributes to the security and efficiency of the checkpoint operation.
preparationPoints: Vehicle stop point and approach warning signs
Document check position and who mans it
How the layout keeps traffic moving and maintains security

title: Infantry Unit Structure
instruction: Describe the organisational structure of a standard infantry unit from section or squad level up to battalion level. For each level, explain how many personnel are typically involved, who is in command, and what that level's main responsibilities are.
preparationPoints: Section or squad — size and NCO command
How each level supports and receives orders from those above and below

title: Forward Operating Base Assessment
instruction: You have just arrived at a forward operating base for an assessment visit. Describe the base's defensive posture, key strengths and vulnerabilities you have observed, and your initial assessment of its adequacy for the mission.
preparationPoints: Location and terrain — advantages and disadvantages
Force protection measures currently in place
Your overall assessment and immediate recommendations

title: Intelligence Threat Assessment
instruction: You have completed an intelligence assessment of the threat environment in your operational area. Brief your commander on the assessment: identify the main threat actors present, describe their estimated capabilities and likely intentions, state your assessment of the most likely course of action they will take against your force or mission, and identify the most significant intelligence gaps that limit your confidence in the assessment.
preparationPoints: Main threat actors and their identities
Likely intentions based on available intelligence
Most likely course of action against your force
Key intelligence gaps that limit confidence

title: Joint Operations Centre Layout
instruction: Describe the layout and function of a joint operations centre or command post you have worked in or are familiar with. Explain where the key functional areas are located, what the principal staff positions are and what each is responsible for, how information flows through the centre, and how decisions are made, recorded, and communicated to subordinate units.
preparationPoints: Physical layout of the operations centre
Key functional areas and their purpose
How information flows into and through the centre
How decisions are made and communicated to subordinate units

title: Operational Area Analysis
instruction: Describe the operational area you are preparing to deploy into for a stability operation. Cover the key terrain features and their military significance, the human terrain — including population structure, political or community authority, and economic conditions — the critical infrastructure your force will depend on or be required to protect, and the main operational constraints these environmental factors impose on your planning.
preparationPoints: Key terrain features and their military significance
Population structure and key community or political authority
Economic conditions and how they affect the mission
Critical infrastructure to protect or depend on
Main operational constraints from environmental factors

title: National Force Contribution
instruction: Describe your country's military contribution to a NATO collective defence or crisis response operation — either an existing contribution or a credible hypothetical one. Cover the types and approximate scale of units or assets contributed, any national caveats that govern how those forces may be employed, the logistic support arrangements, and how your contribution integrates with the broader alliance force structure.
preparationPoints: Types and scale of units or assets contributed
How the contribution integrates with NATO force structure

title: NATO Standing Force Capabilities
instruction: Describe the composition and operational capabilities of one of NATO's standing forces — for example a standing maritime group, the Very High Readiness Joint Task Force, or a multinational corps headquarters. Explain what it consists of, how it is commanded, what kinds of mission it is designed to perform, and what its principal limitations are in terms of scale, readiness, or sustainability.
preparationPoints: Name and composition of the chosen standing force
Mission types it is designed to perform
Principal limitations — scale, sustainability, or capability gaps

title: Training Exercise Account
instruction: Describe a training exercise you participated in recently. Explain what the objectives were, what your role was, what went well, and what lessons were identified at the end.
preparationPoints: Name and type of exercise (tactical, logistics, communications)
Your role and responsibilities during the exercise
A specific challenge or incident during the exercise
What worked well from your perspective
One lesson identified and how it could be applied

title: First International Deployment
instruction: Describe your first experience working alongside military personnel from another country. What surprised you? What did you learn? How did it change the way you approach multinational operations?
preparationPoints: Context — where, when, what kind of activity
Your initial expectations and how they were challenged
A specific interaction that stood out
What you learned about working internationally
How you would approach a similar experience differently now

title: First Aid During Training
instruction: Describe a time when you or a colleague needed first aid during a training activity. Explain what happened, what injury or medical problem occurred, what first aid was given on the spot, and how the situation was resolved.
preparationPoints: The training activity and what you were doing
What happened — the injury or medical problem
What first aid was given immediately
How you or a colleague called for help
The final outcome — treated on site or evacuated

title: Lost Equipment Account
instruction: Describe an experience in which military equipment under your responsibility was reported as lost or missing. Explain the circumstances, how the loss was discovered, what steps you or your unit took to find or account for it, and what the final outcome was.
preparationPoints: What equipment was lost or reported missing
When and how the loss was discovered
Final outcome — found, replaced, or written off

title: A Challenging Patrol
instruction: Describe a patrol or field activity that was more difficult than expected. Explain what made it challenging — whether terrain, weather, equipment failure, or another factor — how your team managed the difficulties, and what you personally learned from the experience.
preparationPoints: What the patrol or activity was and its objective
What made it more difficult than expected
How your team managed the difficulties
A specific challenge your team overcame
What you personally learned from the experience

title: A Language Difficulty at Work
instruction: Describe a time when a language difficulty caused a problem for you during your work or training. Explain what the situation was, what problem the language difficulty caused, and what you or your unit did to manage it.
preparationPoints: The language difficulty — what you did not understand or could not explain
The problem caused by the language difficulty
How you or your unit managed the situation at the time
Whether the situation was resolved and how

title: Navigation Error During Training
instruction: Describe an occasion when your unit or patrol made a navigational error during an operation or training exercise. Explain how the error occurred, what the consequences were, how you identified and corrected the mistake, and what lesson you took from the experience.
preparationPoints: The operation or exercise and your navigation task
The consequences — time lost, wrong area reached
How you identified and corrected the mistake
The lesson learned for future navigation tasks

title: Decision Under Time Pressure
instruction: Describe a situation in which you or a commander you observed had to make a significant decision under time pressure, with incomplete information. What was decided, how, and what was the outcome?
preparationPoints: The situation — what was at stake and why time was critical
What information was available and what was missing
How the decision was made and communicated
The outcome and what it taught you about decision-making

title: Unit Crisis Response
instruction: Describe a serious crisis or emergency that your unit faced during an operation or exercise. Explain how the situation developed, how leadership responded, and what the final outcome was.
preparationPoints: How the crisis began and how quickly it escalated
The immediate response and who took charge
Key decisions made and the reasoning behind them
Coordination with other units or agencies involved
The outcome and key lessons for future operations

title: Working with International Forces
instruction: Describe an experience working alongside forces from a different NATO or partner nation. What professional and cultural differences did you encounter? How did you manage them, and what did you gain from the experience?
preparationPoints: Context of the cooperation — operation, exercise, or liaison
Most significant professional or procedural difference you encountered
A cultural misunderstanding or friction and how it was resolved
What the other force's approach taught you about your own
How the experience changed your approach to joint operations

title: An Ethical Dilemma in Operations
instruction: Describe a situation in which you, or a commander you directly observed, faced a genuine ethical dilemma during an operation or exercise — a situation where the legal order, the ethical requirement, and the immediate needs of your personnel were in tension. Explain what the dilemma was, what decision was made and on what basis, and what the experience taught you about how military leaders should navigate the relationship between law, ethics, and effective command.
preparationPoints: The operational situation and the ethical tension it created
The specific competing obligations — legal, ethical, and personnel welfare
What decision was made and the basis for it
What the experience taught you about ethics and leadership

title: A Successful De-escalation
instruction: Describe a situation you personally observed or participated in where a military officer successfully de-escalated a confrontation or reached an agreement with a difficult interlocutor — a local authority, community leader, or armed group representative. Explain the context, what made the situation difficult, what approach the officer used, and what the outcome demonstrated about the professional skills a military leader needs for operations beyond conventional combat.
preparationPoints: The context — where and what kind of confrontation or negotiation
The specific approach the officer used
The outcome of the de-escalation or negotiation
What this demonstrates about professional military leadership skills

title: An Intelligence Assessment That Failed
instruction: Describe a situation — from your own experience or from documented operational history — in which an intelligence assessment proved to be incorrect, and explain the operational consequences of that failure. Analyse why the assessment was wrong, and draw the key lessons this case illustrates about how commanders should use and critically evaluate intelligence products.
preparationPoints: What was assessed and what the assessment concluded
What actually happened and how it differed from the assessment
The operational consequences of the intelligence failure
Why the assessment was wrong — collection gap, bias, or deception
Lessons for how commanders should evaluate and use intelligence

title: Leading a Multinational Element
instruction: Describe an experience of commanding or serving in a multinational coalition unit — or, if you have not had this experience, describe a documented case you have studied. What were the principal command and control challenges you encountered or observed? How were they managed or resolved? What does this experience or case tell you about what multinational military leadership requires beyond the skills needed for national command?
preparationPoints: The context — what operation or exercise, which nations
A specific moment that illustrated the challenge or its resolution
What multinational leadership requires beyond national command skills

title: A Strategic Communication Failure
instruction: Describe a case — from your own professional experience or from recent operational history — in which a military force's strategic communication failed, resulting in a measurable loss of public or political support for the mission. Analyse what went wrong in the communication strategy, why the failure occurred, and what principles of effective military strategic communication this case illustrates for future commanders.
preparationPoints: The operation and the communication failure that occurred
How and why support was lost
What specifically went wrong in the communication strategy
Why the failure occurred — root cause analysis
Principles of effective strategic communication this case illustrates

title: Day Patrol versus Night Patrol
instruction: Compare a day patrol with a night patrol. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of each? Which would you prefer for a standard reconnaissance mission in an unfamiliar area with no previous intelligence, and why?
preparationPoints: Main advantages of a day patrol
Main disadvantages of a day patrol
Main advantages of a night patrol
Main disadvantages of a night patrol

title: Radio versus Satellite Communication
instruction: Compare the use of a hand-held radio with a satellite communication terminal for a patrol operating in mountainous terrain far from base. Consider range, portability, reliability, and security. Recommend which system is more suitable for this specific scenario and explain your reasoning.
preparationPoints: Reliability in difficult terrain and weather

title: Classroom versus Field Training
instruction: Compare classroom instruction with field training exercises as methods for developing soldiers' tactical skills. What are the main advantages and limitations of each approach? Recommend which method is more effective for preparing a newly formed unit for its first deployment and justify your choice.
preparationPoints: Main advantages of field training exercises
Main limitations of field training exercises
Your recommendation for a newly formed unit and two justifications

title: Convoy versus Helicopter Resupply
instruction: Your unit needs to move supplies and personnel to a remote forward post reachable by road or by helicopter. Compare these two transport options — considering time, capacity, cost, terrain, and security — and recommend which to use for a time-sensitive resupply mission given that air assets are currently limited.
preparationPoints: Time comparison — convoy route vs helicopter flight
